Completion of the measure on the day of the visit rose from 31 to 62 percent in prompt clinics and from 29 to 35 percent in comparison clinics over nine months. Where the measure was completed, clinicians opened the score during the visit in 71 percent of visits. Patients aged over 65 and patients without a smartphone completed the measure less often. Clinics chose whether to take part."},{"title":"Clinician training and audit feedback to increase routine outcome monitoring in community mental health teams: a cluster randomised trial","authors":"Haugland-Obi M, Ferraro-Nkosi D, Lindqvist-Amadi J","year":2021,"venue":"Community Psychiatry Trials","doi":"10.5555/cpt.2021.0044","providerType":"Randomized Controlled Trial","abstract":"Twenty-four community mental health teams were randomised to a clinician training day plus monthly audit feedback on measure use, or to usual practice. At 12 months, the proportion of depression visits with a completed and discussed measure rose from 22 to 41 percent in intervention teams and from 20 to 24 percent in control teams. Depression response at six months did not differ between arms (38 against 36 percent). In the six months after feedback stopped, measure use in intervention teams fell back towards baseline. Fidelity to the feedback schedule varied between teams."},{"title":"Measurement-based care and remission of depression: a systematic review and meta-analysis of controlled studies","authors":"Quintero-Hale A, Obuya-Lindsay P, Kerr-Watanabe S, Mensah-Dubois L","year":2020,"venue":"Evidence Syntheses in Psychiatry","doi":"10.5555/esp.2020.0118","providerType":"review","abstract":"We searched five databases to 2019 for controlled studies comparing measurement-based care with usual care for adults with depression. Fourteen studies met the criteria, nine in outpatient psychiatry and five in primary care. Measurement-based care was associated with a higher chance of remission (risk ratio 1.28, 95 percent CI 1.07 to 1.53), with substantial heterogeneity. Definitions of measurement-based care ranged from routine completion of a measure to protocol-driven treatment changes, and only three studies were set in community mental health services. Risk of bias was high in eight studies."},{"title":"Defining uptake of routine outcome measures: a methodological review of 47 implementation studies","authors":"Brandvold-Achebe T, Salinas-Reyes M","year":2022,"venue":"Implementation Methods Review","providerType":"review","abstract":"We reviewed how 47 studies of routine outcome measurement in mental health defined uptake. We found eleven distinct definitions, from a measure being offered to a measure being completed, reviewed by the clinician and discussed with the patient. Only 9 of the 47 studies required that the clinician review the score. Studies with stricter definitions reported lower uptake. Denominators also varied: visits, patients or episodes of care. We propose a core definition of uptake as a completed measure reviewed by the clinician at the same visit, with visits as the denominator."},{"title":"What patients say about completing depression questionnaires before appointments","authors":"Adair-Nwosu K, Fontaine-Mbeki G","year":2019,"venue":"Service User Perspectives","providerType":"qualitative","abstract":"We spoke with 28 adults receiving outpatient treatment for depression about completing a symptom questionnaire before each appointment. Most found it quick and valued it when the clinician discussed the score with them. Several stopped completing it when the score was never mentioned, describing the form as paperwork for the clinic rather than for them. Some worried about how honest answers would be used. Participants suggested that the clinician should show them the trend over time. Participants were recruited from two clinics with high measure use."},{"title":"Routine symptom measurement and treatment changes in outpatient depression care: an analysis of routinely collected data","authors":"Okwuosa-Brennan F, Delacourt-Singh H","year":2017,"venue":"Journal of Measurement in Mental Health Care","doi":"10.5555/jmmhc.2017.0023","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"Using routinely collected data for 9,400 outpatients with depression, we examined visits at which the patient's score had not improved since the previous visit. Treatment was changed at 39 percent of such visits when the score had been completed and viewed by the clinician, against 24 percent when no score was available (odds ratio 1.9, 95 percent CI 1.6 to 2.3). The association held across clinicians with different overall measure use. We could not tell whether the treatment changes improved outcomes."},{"title":"Sustaining measurement-based care after implementation support ends: two-year follow-up in eight clinics","authors":"Ruiz-Halvorsen N, Takahashi-Moyo E, Pereira-Grant J","year":2025,"venue":"Implementation Methods Review","doi":"10.5555/imr.2025.0036","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"Eight outpatient clinics received 12 months of external implementation support for measurement-based care, including training, electronic prompts and quarterly feedback. Completion of the measure at depression visits reached 58 percent at the end of support and fell to 39 percent one year later. Clinics that had appointed a local clinical champion kept completion above 50 percent, while clinics without one fell below 30 percent. Clinician turnover was associated with the decline, and clinics that stopped reviewing scores in team meetings lost completion fastest. There was no comparison group, so secular change cannot be excluded."},{"title":"Measurement feedback in depression care across primary and specialist settings: report of a conference symposium","authors":"Outcome Measurement Forum Working Group","year":null,"venue":"Proceedings of the Outcome Measurement Forum","providerType":"conference-report","abstract":"This report summarises seven presentations from a symposium on measurement feedback in depression care. Presenters described electronic prompts, clinician dashboards, patient-held score charts and payment incentives in primary care and specialist services. Several reported increases in measure completion after new systems were introduced, but quantitative results are not given in the report. Speakers agreed that feedback to clinicians without protected time to act on it had little effect. The report does not state the year of the symposium or how presentations were selected."}]}
